source_span: Central bankers tend to correct (and often overcorrect) for the last crisis. In 2022 the consensus view was they didn't react quickly enough to high inflation. We're already seeing a more hawkish reaction function this time around.
source_chain: Central banks systematically overcorrect for the mistake of the prior cycle (dovish after 2008, now hawkish after being 'too late' on 2021-23 inflation), and markets have a documented history of underpricing hiking-cycle scope at the outset (1994: 140bps priced by Christmas vs 300bps delivered over the year; 2022: 200bps priced vs 400bps delivered) — therefore fresh commodity/energy price gains not yet reflected in inflation data, combined with this overcorrecting reaction function, mean the 2026 cycle is also likely underpriced — therefore investors should expect more/faster hikes than futures currently show ('the hawkish risk'). DB states no explicit falsifiable invalidation for this thesis, only a consequence caveat (if growth/earnings stay resilient, risk assets need not suffer even so, per the 1999 precedent).
pulse_chain: The Fed's first hike in three years to 3.75-4.00% (unanimous) leaves ~75bps more priced by June (DB) — therefore markets have undepriced hikes before, citing DB's own 1994 (300bps vs 140bps) and 2022 (400bps vs 200bps) figures, reinforced by the oil-10yr correlation hitting a 35-year high (Cboe), making energy a direct amplifier of the rate path — therefore Goldman's short-cycle call (one more hike then flat, resting on cooling core PCE) is undercut by the actual August print (core PCE accelerated on an oil-driven shock) and by a Fed reaction function that has structurally turned hawkish (DB's overcorrection argument) — invalidation: the 10-year (4.99%) closing decisively above 5% before the Oct 27-28 meeting confirms the hawkish case, with BTIG's 4.92% as the level that flips it back.
why: The pulse reproduces DB's two load-bearing planks — the exact historical underpricing figures (1994 140/300bps, 2022 200/400bps) and the reaction-function overcorrection story — correctly attributed to Deutsche Bank, and layers Goldman's counter-case and a BTIG-sourced invalidation on top without misattributing them to DB or reversing DB's direction, which is permissible synthesis since DB's own note supplies no invalidation to swap out.
